Join the Mathematics Expert Talent Network | Global Remote 📐🧮
What This Pool Covers,
Pure and applied mathematics; abstract algebra and topology
Real and complex analysis; discrete mathematics and combinatorics
Probability theory and statistics; mathematical modeling and optimization
(Where you trained matters less than whether you can tell a proof from a convincing sketch, and say precisely where the gap is.)

The research teams behind the best-known AI models come to Mercor for mathematical judgment they can't generate on their own. Instead of posting and pulling listings every time a new initiative kicks off, we maintain a standing mathematics talent pool to draw from on short notice.
💰 Compensation: Most contracts in this field have paid $40 to $75 an hour, set per project by scope and depth.

What the Work Looks Like

Problem Creation: Writing a problem at research or competition level—with statements, intended solutions, and reference answers.

Proof Grading: Evaluating model-written proofs (checking if steps follow logically, edge cases are handled, and theorem hypotheses are satisfied).

Gap Analysis Flagging: Identifying where a model reaches a correct final answer through a flawed argument or convincing sketch that doesn't actually prove it.

What We're Looking For

A graduate degree in mathematics or a related field, or an equivalent research or competition background

Clear written communication (since most work involves explaining your reasoning)

Comfort with ambiguous tasks, and willingness to flag unclear instructions

How It Works

Apply: Submit your resume via the link in Comments and confirm your location.

AI Interview: Take a short, ~20-minute AI interview to verify your background.

Get Matched: When a project needs mathematics expertise, we invite matching people from the pool to that specific listing. It names the rate, the hours, and the client, and any hiring decision is made there.

(Note: This is a standing pool, so this listing does not send out rejections. We reach out whenever a project matches your background, which could be within a week or a few months.)

💡 How to Apply: Check the link in the comments to view full details and submit your application!
📝 Important: Mention Amit Sharma as your internal referral during the application or screening process!

🤝 Connect / Follow me and drop a "Hi" in DM if you have questions! 💬✨

Best Regards,
Amit Sharma

Position Overview

We are hiring a Senior Software Engineer to help expand WorkPro, our flagship operations platform deployed across multiple client environments. You will work in a small, senior team, own services end-to-end across the stack, and help shape the technical direction of a system used daily by real operational teams.

This role is perfect for an experienced full-stack engineer who enjoys solving complex workflow problems, building reliable APIs, and working across modern and legacy systems.

What You'll Do

Backend & Integrations

· Build and maintain REST APIs using Java (Spring Boot), Python (Django/FastAPI), .NET (C#/ASP.NET), Golang, or comparable frameworks, powering dispatch, service orders, billing, and asset workflows.
· Design relational schemas, migrations, and high-performance queries against SQL Server and PostgreSQL.

· 5+ years of professional development experience (backend/API focus).

· Solid SQL experience relational modeling, complex queries, indexing, stored procedures.
· Practical experience with an ORM (JPA/Hibernate, Entity Framework, SQLAlchemy, GORM, or equivalent) and migration tooling (Flyway, Liquibase, Alembic, or similar).
· Experience maintaining and refactoring legacy codebases.
· Experience integrating with enterprise systems (ERP/CRM).
· Comfort with concurrency, messaging, and asynchronous processing (Kafka, RabbitMQ, or similar).
· Testing discipline (JUnit/Mockito, pytest, xUnit/NUnit, Testcontainers, or equivalent depending on stack).
· Basic working knowledge of Angular + TypeScript for occasional frontend contributions.

· Comfortable working in a collaborative, agile consulting environment.

Most agencies do not struggle to grow because they cannot sell.

They struggle because every new client creates a delivery and cash-flow problem.

You land a web design or SEO contract, then immediately need specialists, software, project management, quality control, and upfront fulfilment cash.

That is why agency infrastructure matters more than simply “outsourcing.”

Here are 4 ways to build a delivery model that can scale:

1. Productise what you sell

Custom scopes create custom delivery problems.

Define clear packages with specific deliverables, timelines, revision limits, responsibilities, and outcomes.

For example, do not sell “SEO services.”

Sell a defined monthly local SEO system: technical monitoring, Google Business Profile optimisation, location pages, content, reporting, and a fixed review process.

Clear scope protects margin and makes fulfilment repeatable.

2. Separate client strategy from production

Your client should experience your agency’s strategy, communication, quality standards, and accountability.

The technical work can be delivered by trusted specialists, contractors, or white-label partners.

But do not outsource your relationship with the client.

Own the brief, the goals, the reporting, the quality check, and the next recommendation. That is where agency value compounds.

3. Match cost structure to revenue timing

Hiring a full-time team before revenue is stable creates fixed costs that keep running even when client work slows down.

A flexible delivery network lets you pay for capacity when work is sold, rather than carrying every specialist on payroll from day one.

The key is not avoiding investment.

It is avoiding fixed overhead before you have repeatable demand and reliable margins.

4. Build systems your client can trust

A white-label dashboard, consistent onboarding, project milestones, approval workflows, reporting templates, and documented processes make a small agency feel organised without pretending to be a large one.

Clients do not pay for the size of your team.

They pay for clarity, progress, results, and confidence that someone is accountable.

The biggest mistake is treating white-label fulfilment as a shortcut.

It is infrastructure.

If your offers, vendor standards, quality control, and client communication are weak, outsourcing will only scale the inconsistency.

But when the system is clear, flexible fulfilment gives you room to grow without turning every new sale into an operational emergency.

If you are building a web design, SEO, or AI automation agency and want to scale delivery without losing control of quality or margins, send me a message. I can help you structure a simple offer, fulfilment workflow, and client experience before you add more overhead.

Two interviews. Five years apart. Same reason they both fail.

Room 1. SDET interview, 2021.
The candidate knows Playwright cold. Built three frameworks. Open
source contributor. Answers "how do you structure a page object"
flawlessly.
Then the interviewer asks: "A defect gets past your regression
suite on release day. Walk me through your first hour."
Silence.

Room 2. AI/LLM engineer interview, 2026.
The candidate fine-tuned models. Deployed RAG. Wrote a blog post
on tool calling that hit 200k reads.
Then the interviewer asks: "Your retrieval returns confident wrong
answers under load. Walk me through how you debug the pipeline."
Same silence.

Two different rooms. Same problem: rehearsed knowledge without
rehearsed performance.
I've been on the hiring side for 15 years — Amazon, Visa,
PlayStation, Paytm. Ran 100+ bar-raiser interviews for SDET roles.
The pattern never changed. Candidates who practice daily
outperform candidates who study weekends. Every time.

So I built DailyKnack — a 15-minute daily loop for both rooms.

→ 9 MCQs
→ 1 spoken answer
→ 1 code rep
→ 1 Code Review Drill

Two tracks live today:
• SDET — web automation, API contracts, test data, CI/CD,
  performance, accessibility, contract testing
• AI/LLM Engineering — RAG, context engineering, tool calling,
  memory, evals, multi-agent systems, MCP

Every question is curated from real interviews. Answers are
drafted with AI and reviewed by me — same bar I used as a
bar-raiser.

Anonymous by design. No email, no name. Free tier stays free.
No card, no trial.

https://dailyknack.in

missing.

Boards are accelerating AI adoption for enterprise decisions — procurement, risk assessment, workforce planning. The promise is faster, data-driven choices. But a pattern is emerging across boardrooms in 2026: boards delegate authority to systems they cannot audit, built on reasoning they cannot see, producing outcomes they cannot explain.

The governance gap is not whether the AI was accurate. It is who answers when it is wrong. A vendor contract awarded on opaque scoring. A hiring algorithm that winnows without a visible rule. Risk models that flag accounts for closure with no documented rationale. Each decision carries the board's authority, but the board did not make it, cannot retrace it, and in most cases cannot even ask the system how it reached its conclusion.

That gap is the definition of ungoverned delegation, and it is standard practice. When a decision cannot be traced back to its inputs, accountability becomes decorative. Accountability flows upward until it doesn't. AI is where the chain stops.

This is the layer collective intelligence exists to hold open. Not a cleaner algorithm, but a record where the reasoning survives contact with the decision. We opened the room on it today. When a board delegates to AI it cannot audit, who holds the AI accountable?

I negotiated my first $4,000/month remote contract through LinkedIn.
No job board.
No Upwork.
No “Are you hiring?” messages.
Just content → conversation → contract.

Here’s how it happened:
1. I posted consistently for some time.
Nothing viral.
Just specific Android engineering content around architecture, performance, and real production problems.
A UK fintech founder noticed my posts and reached out.

2. The first call wasn't about my rate.
I asked about their product, team, bottlenecks, and what they were struggling with.
I listened.
By the end, I understood the problem I could solve.

3. I sold the outcome, not my hours.
Instead of sending a CV, I sent a one-page proposal:
Their problem → My solution → Expected outcome → Rate

4. They pushed back on the price.
I didn't discount.
We talked about the cost of leaving the problem unsolved.

5. I offered a 2-week paid trial.
Same rate. Low commitment for them.
The trial turned into a 6-month contract.

The biggest lesson?

Content got me noticed.
The conversation built trust.
The proposal made the value clear.
The trial made saying yes easy.
That's the system.

The conversation around design in 2026 is shifting away from pixel-perfect mockups toward something far more structural: the interface as a machine-readable contract.

The most overlooked trend is the rise of Machine Experience Design, or MX. When an AI agent interacts with your product—to book a meeting, file a ticket, or update a record—it does not see the gradient or the animation. It reads the semantic HTML, the accessible labels, the data attributes behind each component. If your design system does not expose a structured schema alongside the visual layer, your interface becomes invisible to the agents your users are already delegating work to.

A non-obvious consequence of this shift is how it changes the design-to-development handoff. The next generation of design tools will need to export both a visual spec and a structured data contract that defines how an AI agent should interact with each element. This is not an accessibility overlay. It is a new design primitive. Teams that invest in this now will build products that are discoverable and usable by both humans and machines, which is the only path to scale in an agentic world.

Another change hiding in the 2026 trends is the move toward emotionally aware, reactive interfaces. The bold color palettes and adaptive layouts are not just aesthetic choices. They are reactive to context, user state, and even biometric feedback. But the real insight is not the technology. It is the ethical design challenge it creates. When your interface changes based on a user's emotional state, you are no longer a designer. You are a behavioral architect. The teams that will succeed are the ones that define clear boundaries for when and how this reactivity is triggered, and who audit for dark patterns before they ship.

For hiring managers evaluating senior design talent: the engineers and designers who understand MX and reactive context design are the ones who can build systems that work for both end-users and the AI agents acting on their behalf. They do not just make things look good. They design interfaces that are semantically rigorous, ethically grounded, and structurally discoverable. These are the people who will lead the next wave of product design.

How is your team preparing for the shift toward designing interfaces that must be readable by both humans and AI agents?

I’m currently looking for an experienced Data Scientist – ML & AI for a 6-month contract role (extendable) with an opportunity to work on end-to-end AI/ML solutions.

🔹 Experience: 6–8+ Years(Mandatory)
🔹 Location: Remote
🔹 Employment: Contract – 6 Months, Extendable
🔹 Compensation: ₹0.78 – ₹0.98 LPM

🔍 What We’re Looking For

The ideal candidate should have strong, hands-on experience across:
✅ Machine Learning & Data Science
✅ Statistical Modelling
✅ Python & SQL
✅ Data Analysis & Feature Engineering
✅ Experimentation using large/complex datasets
✅ End-to-End ML/AI Model Deployment
✅ Cloud & Data Platforms
✅ MLOps
✅ Production Model Monitoring & Optimization
✅ Cross-functional collaboration with Client, Consulting & Engineering teams

⭐ Preferred: Experience with generative AI, LLMs and agentic AI

⚠️ Important
This opportunity is specifically for candidates who have genuine hands-on project experience and can independently contribute to the complete Data Science/AI lifecycle — from data exploration and model development through production deployment and optimization.

If your experience is primarily theoretical or limited to POCs/training projects, this role may not be the right fit.

📩 Interested candidates:
DM me with your updated CV + current location + notice period + expected compensation. @harishhsamrajan@outlook.com 
If you know someone who fits the profile, please tag them or share this post.
